title: Seeing Through the Glare: A Multi-Source Benchmark and Ocular-Adaptive Pixel MeanFlow for Eyeglass Reflection Removal

paper.title: Seeing Through the Glare: A Multi-Source Benchmark and Ocular-Adaptive Pixel MeanFlow for Eyeglass Reflection Removal

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reflections from windows or monitors on eyeglasses can obscure the eyes while leaving most of a portrait intact. Although spatially confined, this interference can noticeably change facial appearance in photographs and video communication. Its effects range from color shifts over visible structures to severe occlusion of the iris, eyelids, and eyelashes [ 1 , 2 ] . A single image may therefore require photometric correction in some regions, content reconstruction in others, and faithful preservation elsewhere. Accommodating these different restoration needs is essential to removing reflections without unnecessarily changing the portrait. Despite progress in eyeglass reflection removal [ 3 , 1 , 2 ] , challenges remain in obtaining reliable supervision and evaluation data and balancing restoration accuracy with inference efficiency. At the data level, limitations are threefold: (1) head motion, blinking, and illumination changes compromise pixel-level correspondence in captured pairs [ 1 ] ; (2) synthetic pairs provide controlled correspondence and degradation but cannot alone establish performance under natural reflections; and (3) real-input pseudo-pairs retain natural reflections, but the true appearance of obscured ocular content cannot be verified from reflected inputs alone. Therefore, reliable assessment requires complementary sources and real-world evaluation independent of generated targets. At the model level, reconstructing obscured ocular structures requires expressive priors, while applications demand efficient inference. Diffusion models [ 4 ] , DiT [ 5 ] , and SiT [ 6 ] demonstrate strong image synthesis capabilities. These models typically rely on iterative sampling with multiple network evaluations. MeanFlow [ 7 ] learns average velocities over time intervals for single-evaluation generation, while pMF [ 8 ] combines image prediction with velocity-space learning for one-step generation without a latent autoencoder. Although pMF provides an efficient foundation for one-step generation, applying it to eyeglass reflection removal requires aligning generative computation with spatially heterogeneous restoration demands. Under a limited token budget, uniform tokenization allocates computation to largely unaffected regions while providing insufficient resolution for fine ocular structures. Within the lenses, similar reflection intensities may leave different amounts of ocular structure visible, indicating that reflection strength alone cannot determine restoration requirements. Therefore, effective reconstruction requires guidance from both local observations and ocular geometry. In addition, compact patch representations can discard native photographic details, whereas directly preserving observed high-frequency content risks retaining reflection artifacts. To address these challenges, we introduce OcuBench , a multi-source benchmark for eyeglass reflection removal. OcuBench comprises 10,280 synthetic pairs, 732 real-input pseudo-pairs, and 458 independently collected real-world test images. Synthetic pairs vary in subject, imaging, and reflection factors. Real-input pseudo-pairs combine real reflected inputs with generated clean targets. The real-world set evaluates performance beyond generated supervision, with clean references for a subset. These sources support development and evaluation under controlled and real-world conditions. Based on OcuBench, we develop OcuFlow , an efficient ocular-adaptive pMF framework for eyeglass reflection removal. OcuFlow uses geometry-adaptive supports under a fixed token budget to concentrate resolution on ocular structures while preserving coarse context. The supports retain position and scale information to preserve spatial correspondence. A geometry-guided pMF integrates local reflected observations, ocular priors, and cross-scale features to restore pixel patches in one forward pass. A native-resolution frequency-preserving renderer projects predictions to the supplied input resolution. The renderer selectively blends predictions with observations across frequency bands to preserve photographic details and reduce unnecessary modifications. Experiments show that OcuFlow achieves superior overall restoration quality on the held-out paired benchmark compared with existing methods. OcuFlow runs in 56 ms per image on an RTX 4090 GPU, providing 4 4 – 66 × 66\times speedups over the compared methods under the same evaluation protocol. Independent real-world evaluation further shows competitive no-reference performance, and OcuFlow achieves the highest user preference in the user study. Beyond image-level restoration metrics, we evaluate downstream iris localization using a fixed detector without fine-tuning. OcuFlow achieves the best both-eyes localization accuracy among the compared method, demonstrating that its restoration benefits extend to downstream ocular analysis. These results demonstrate the potential of OcuFlow for efficient and detail-preserving portrait restoration.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Eyeglass Reflection Removal and Benchmarks. EwE [ 3 ] overlays reflection patches on frontal portraits, while De-Glared [ 9 ] constructs 2,541 synthetic pairs from generated portraits. ReyeR [ 1 ] provides filtered, color-corrected real pairs across varied conditions. Synthetic realism and real-pair alignment remain challenges. Methods span constrained optimization [ 3 ] , supervised restoration [ 10 , 9 ] , and generative facial reconstruction [ 11 ] . ER 2 Net [ 1 ] fuses reflection removal and inpainting by reflection intensity, while DL2G [ 2 ] combines degradation correction, local structure-aware diffusion, and global refinement. We introduce a multi-source benchmark and efficient restoration for portrait editing and video communication. Spatially Adaptive Visual Representations. Adaptive visual representations improve efficiency through token aggregation, conditional computation, and spatially varying resolution. TokenLearner [ 12 ] aggregates dense features into fewer adaptive tokens, while A-ViT [ 13 ] dynamically halts token processing at different network depths. Mixed-Resolution Tokenization [ 14 ] constructs variable-sized patches through saliency-guided quadtree partitioning, whereas MSViT [ 15 ] uses learned gating to select patch scales with input-dependent token counts. For eyeglass restoration, spatial allocation must resolve fine ocular structures while maintaining correspondence with the original image. OcuFlow uses input-derived ocular geometry to optimize quadtree partitioning under a fixed token budget, concentrating resolution on critical eye structures. Each token retains its position and scale for geometry-guided restoration and native-resolution reconstruction. Generative Restoration. Generative priors support restoration from incomplete observations. Diffusion [ 4 ] and Flow Matching [ 16 ] typically require iterative sampling. DifFace [ 17 ] reconstructs faces with pretrained diffusion, while DiffBIR [ 18 ] combines degradation removal with diffusion-based detail regeneration. GFP-GAN [ 19 ] enables single-pass restoration using pretrained facial GAN priors. CodeFormer [ 20 ] predicts discrete codes with a controllable fidelity–quality trade-off. Dereflection Any Image [ 21 ] adopts one-step diffusion for reflection removal. MeanFlow [ 7 ] learns average velocities over time intervals for single-evaluation generation. pMF [ 8 ] combines image prediction with velocity-space learning for one-step pixel-space generation. We adapt it to conditional restoration over ocular-adaptive patches. One-step restoration addresses efficiency , but not what to restore and preserve . WaveFace [ 22 ] uses diffusion for low-frequency wavelet components and a feed-forward network for high-frequency recovery. Our renderer blends predictions with native-resolution observations by frequency, selectively retaining reliable high-frequency details beyond compact patches. sections.heading: 3 OcuBench: A Multi-Source Benchmark
sections.text: Tab. 1 compares representative eyeglass reflection datasets by construction, pairing, scale, and access. Controlled real capture provides physically valid paired observations, while synthetic composition enables scalable and controllable variation in reflection patterns. However, large-scale real paired facial data are difficult to collect and release due to acquisition constraints and privacy concerns, whereas synthetic data alone cannot fully capture naturally occurring reflections. OcuBench therefore combines controllable synthetic pairs, real-input pseudo-pairs, and independent real-world samples, leveraging their complementary strengths for controlled degradation analysis, realistic reflection coverage, and independent real-world evaluation. The following subsections describe data collection, generation, cleaning, and quality control, with further procedural details in appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.2 Data Cleaning and Quality Control
sections.text: Ocu-P Input Screening. For the SoF dataset, CLIP-based reflection screening [ 25 ] followed by manual inspection yields 199 images. For the Web data, FaceMesh-guided local-highlight screening in estimated eye regions yields 1,740 candidates from 11,520 retrieved images, with manual inspection further reducing them to 533. The resulting 732 images are used to generate pseudo-clean targets. Ocu-S and Ocu-P Validation. GPT-Image-2 generates synthetic pairs under shared scene constraints, whereas real-input editing must preserve the photograph while inferring obscured content. Both risk pairwise structural drift in facial or ocular geometry. An edge-consistency filter is applied to detect contour changes unrelated to reflections. Four reviewers assess realism, identity and ocular consistency, and preservation of unaffected content, accepting pairs by consensus. We retain 10,280 samples in Ocu-S ( 𝒟 syn \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{syn}} ) and 732 in Ocu-P ( 𝒟 pseudo \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pseudo}} ). Pseudo-clean supervision remains approximate because obscured ocular appearance cannot be verified from reflected inputs alone. Sampling configurations, prompt templates, and filtering criteria appear in appendix A . Ocu-R Reference-pair Processing. Following ReyeR [ 1 ] , we filter candidate captures with large spatial discrepancies using image differences and apply color correction to reduce capture-induced illumination shifts. Of the 200 candidate pairs, 157 are retained, comprising 62 offline and 95 video-conferencing pairs. Residual local misalignment remains, so the clean captures serve as visual references rather than pixel-accurate ground truth. Together with the 301 unpaired images, these form the 458-image Ocu-R. sections.heading: 3.3 Dataset Analysis
sections.text: Reflection and Occlusion Distributions. Fig. 3 (a) summarizes requested reflection configurations in Ocu-S. Screen and light reflections account for 32.6% and 38.6% of samples, respectively, while rectangular patterns are the most common shape at 45.0%. Target ocular occlusion is approximately balanced across mild, moderate, strong, and severe levels, each representing 24.9–25.2% of samples. Reflection strength follows a distinct distribution, with mild and severe cases accounting for 37.8% and 12.9%, respectively. These statistics describe sampled generation settings. Imaging Conditions. Fig. 3 (b) summarizes the imaging configurations. Selfies account for 38.4% of Ocu-S. Scene compositions include direct, mirror, and through-glass views across indoor, outdoor, and vehicle settings. The four target background-blur levels are approximately balanced, spanning sharp to defocused backgrounds. These configurations vary the photographic context around reflected eye regions. Cross-source Image Statistics. Fig. 3 (c) compares the data sources through empirical cumulative distributions of resolution, aspect ratio, luminance, contrast, Laplacian variance, and color saturation. Ocu-R reaches substantially higher resolutions than Ocu-S and Ocu-P, while Ocu-S generally exhibits lower luminance. The three sources also differ in aspect ratio, high-frequency detail, and saturation, but show more similar contrast distributions. These differences highlight source-dependent variation and motivate separate evaluation on independently captured images. Dataset Splits, Evaluation, and Access. We separately split Ocu-S ( 𝒟 syn \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{syn}} ) and Ocu-P ( 𝒟 pseudo \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pseudo}} ) into 60% training and 40% test subsets, then merge the respective splits to form the final training and test sets. Held-out paired evaluation is performed on the merged test set. All 458 Ocu-R inputs are evaluated using no-reference metrics, with 30 randomly selected for a blind user study, while the 157 clean captures support qualitative analysis. We plan to release the synthetic and SoF components directly, release the Web-sourced component upon permission, and provide self-collected data through verified academic access (Tab. 1 ).

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: Given an arbitrary-resolution image with eyeglass reflections I g ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 I_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} , OcuFlow estimates a reflection-free image I out I_{\mathrm{out}} at the same spatial resolution as the input, we denote the clean training target by I 0 I_{0} . As illustrated in Fig. 4 , the method coordinates three decisions: where to allocate capacity, how to restore efficiently, and what to preserve . Ocular geometry determines the spatial supports of a fixed number of pixel patches. A geometry-guided pMF restores the patches in one pass, while a frequency-preserving renderer fuses the predictions with native-resolution observations. Figure 4 : Overview of OcuFlow. Ocular priors guide allocation of 256 tokens. Geometry, reflected observations, and coarse context condition one-step patch restoration. Frequency-preserving synthesis blends predictions with native details within soft lens support.

sections.heading: 5.1 Metrics and Implementation Details
sections.text: Paired evaluation uses Mask-PSNR/SSIM, Mixed-PSNR/SSIM, Eye-ROI LPIPS, and Eye-NME/Iris-NME. Eyeglass masks are initialized with Grounded-SAM-2 [ 26 ] and manually corrected, while NME is computed from MediaPipe landmarks [ 27 ] . Evaluation on Ocu-R comprises NIQE [ 28 ] , CLIP-IQA+ [ 29 ] , and a blind user study. All methods use 1008 × 1296 1008\times 1296 inputs for paired inference and efficiency evaluation on the same RTX 4090. Runtime is measured as the steady-state average wall-clock processing time per image under sustained inference, with each method evaluated using the same throughput-oriented protocol. Paired metrics are computed at the original paired resolutions, while Ocu-R is evaluated at its original resolution. Metric definitions, baseline configurations, training objectives, and efficiency measurement protocols are provided in § C.1 . sections.heading: 5.2 Evaluation
sections.text: Quantitative Results. In Tab. 2 , OcuFlow shows clear advantages in restoration accuracy and efficiency. It ranks first on six of the seven restoration and ocular geometry metrics and achieves a 4.3 × 4.3\times speedup in steady-state processing over ER 2 Net, the second-fastest method under the same evaluation protocol. On Ocu-R ( Fig. 5 (a)), OcuFlow achieves the lowest NIQE (5.2369) and second-highest CLIP-IQA+ (0.6419) among restoration methods. Since the reflected input itself obtains a higher CLIP-IQA+ score (0.6556), we treat no-reference metrics as auxiliary indicators. In the blind user study ( Fig. 5 (b)), OcuFlow receives 67.32% of valid selections and ranks first on 26 of the 30 images. The 95% cluster-bootstrap confidence interval for its preference share is [ 59.32 % , 74.71 % ] [59.32\%,74.71\%] . Beyond image-quality evaluation, downstream iris localization further shows that reflection removal improves the reliability of ocular analysis, with OcuFlow achieving strong bilateral iris-localization performance. Additional analyses and downstream task results are provided in § C.2 and C.3 . Figure 6 : Qualitative comparison. Close-ups highlight reflection removal, ocular reconstruction, and detail preservation. Qualitative Results. Fig. 6 compares results under localized glare and broad blue reflections. RDNet and ReflexSplit retain lens haze in the first example. In the second example, DSIT and ReflexSplit produce softer, lower-contrast eyes, while RDNet retains a blue-purple cast. DL2G introduces irregular details around the rims and eyelids. OcuFlow suppresses dominant reflections in both cases, recovering clearer iris and eyelid contours closer to the references while preserving reliable facial details. Additional results appear in § C.4 .

Tab. 3 (a) shows that ocular-adaptive allocation improves masked reconstruction, Eye-ROI LPIPS, and both ocular NME measures over a uniform grid. Out-PSNR and Out-HF-PSNR remain nearly unchanged, indicating that the gains primarily concern ocular restoration. Removing geometry embedding reduces reconstruction and ocular fidelity, supporting explicit encoding of token position and scale. The uniform grid remains faster, so adaptive allocation trades additional processing time for improved restoration quality. How to Restore Efficiently. Removing either the geometry-aware source or coarse-to-fine conditioning worsens masked reconstruction and all eye-specific metrics in Tab. 3 (b). These results support combining local observations with geometric and contextual guidance. A single network function evaluation (1-NFE) achieves better masked reconstruction and ocular geometry than two evaluations (2-NFE), while requiring less runtime. Although 2-NFE achieves lower Eye-ROI LPIPS, its additional computation does not consistently improve restoration. The 1-NFE setting therefore provides a favorable balance between reconstruction accuracy, ocular fidelity, and efficiency. What to Preserve. Residual rendering improves masked reconstruction and outside-mask agreement over Direct PMF but slightly worsens ocular geometry. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We present OcuBench and OcuFlow, a multi-source benchmark and an ocular-adaptive pMF framework for eyeglass reflection removal. OcuBench combines synthetic pairs, real-input pseudo-pairs, and independent real-world evaluation beyond generated targets. OcuFlow aligns a fixed token budget with ocular geometry and couples one-step restoration with frequency-preserving synthesis to reconstruct obscured eyes while retaining reliable native details. Experiments demonstrate improved reflection removal and ocular-structure reconstruction, leading to more accurate downstream iris localization, while achieving favorable human perceptual preferences on independent real-world images at substantially lower inference cost. Our findings suggest that adapting representation to local needs and selectively preserving observations support effective one-step portrait restoration. Future work could extend this approach to temporally consistent video restoration.

sections.heading: A.2.1 Real Reflected-input Collection
sections.text: For the SoF subset, we start from 2,662 images and perform CLIP-based [ 25 ] reflection screening using CLIP ViT-B/32. To emphasize localized lens reflections while retaining global semantic context, we combine the full-image and periocular-region CLIP features with weights of 0.4 0.4 and 0.6 0.6 , respectively. The text representation is constructed from a multi-prompt ensemble covering five semantic categories: lens reflection, clear eyeglasses, frame highlight, sunglasses, and no glasses. For each image, we compute a reflection margin as the cosine similarity to the reflection prototype minus the highest similarity among the four negative categories, and rank all images accordingly. The top 400 candidates are manually reviewed, yielding 199 images with genuine eyeglass-lens reflections. These 199 images are used for clean-target generation and retained in the final SoF pseudo-pair subset. Table 6 : Construction of the real reflected-input subset. Automatic screening uses CLIP ranking for SoF and FaceMesh-guided reflection screening for Web images. Source Initial Automatic Manual Final SoF 2,662 400 199 199 Web 11,520 1,740 533 533 Total 14,182 2,140 732 732 For the Web subset, we retrieve 11,520 images from Pexels using eyeglass-reflection-related portrait queries. MediaPipe FaceMesh [ 27 ] is used to localize the face and estimate the left and right lens regions from periocular landmarks. Within the estimated lens regions, we compute a local glare score that combines the proportions of low-saturation bright pixels and highly bright pixels, the number and area of valid highlight connected components, and the peak intensity. We retain candidates with a glare score of at least 0.58 0.58 , a white-highlight ratio of at least 0.006 0.006 , a bright-pixel ratio of at least 0.010 0.010 , and at least one valid highlight component. This automatic screening reduces the pool from 11,520 to 1,740 images. We then manually remove false positives caused by eye whites, skin or eyeglass-frame highlights, and other non-lens bright regions, as well as images without clear lens reflections, with opaque or heavily tinted lenses, or with insufficient facial or eyeglass detail. This results in 533 Web images, all of which are retained in the final pseudo-pair set after target generation and pair-level quality control. sections.heading: A.2.2 Clean-target Generation
sections.text: For each retained real reflected input I r real I_{r}^{\mathrm{real}} , we keep the original image unchanged and use GPT-Image-2 to generate the missing reflection-free target I ~ c \widetilde{I}_{c} at the same resolution as the input. If an editing call fails, the request is retried after a 20-second delay, with at most five total attempts per input. If all five attempts fail, the corresponding sample is discarded and processing proceeds to the next input. In practice, no input exhausted the five-attempt budget, and all retained real reflected inputs were successfully paired with generated clean targets. The original reflected image is used directly as the input of each pseudo-pair, while GPT-Image-2 is applied only to obtain its missing clean counterpart. The editing instruction removes lens reflections while preserving identity, facial and ocular structure, pose, eyeglass geometry, background, composition, and overall photographic appearance. A representative prompt template is shown below. Reflection-removal prompt template Preserve the person, pose, eyeglasses, background, and composition. Remove reflections only from the eyeglass lenses, recover clear and realistic eyes, and maintain a natural photographic appearance. Do not modify identity, facial geometry, eyeglass geometry, or any non-reflection content. The generated image is used exclusively as the pseudo-clean target I ~ c \widetilde{I}_{c} ; the reflected member of the pair remains the original real image I r real I_{r}^{\mathrm{real}} without generative modification. This asymmetric construction ensures that the reflection distribution in the pseudo-pairs is inherited directly from real observations rather than from the image generator.

sections.heading: A.2.3 Pseudo-pair Filtering
sections.text: We apply the same registration-aware, mask-aware edge-consistency filtering procedure described in § A.1.3 to assess structural agreement between each real reflected input and its generated pseudo-clean target. Pairs are subsequently reviewed by four reviewers for identity drift, facial or ocular deformation, eyeglass-frame distortion, changes in pose or gaze, background or composition changes, incomplete reflection removal, and unintended modifications outside the lens regions. A pseudo-pair is retained only with unanimous agreement among all four reviewers. The 732 reflected inputs retained after input screening, comprising 199 images from SoF and 533 from the Web subset, are used for clean-target generation. In practice, none of the resulting pseudo-pairs were rejected during pair-level quality control, and all 732 were retained in the final Ocu-P set.

sections.heading: A.3.1 Reference-pair Capture and Processing
sections.text: We collect 200 candidate reflected–clean pairs through two complementary acquisition protocols, comprising 100 offline pairs captured under controlled indoor conditions and 100 online pairs collected through remote video sessions. For the offline subset, images are captured with an iPhone in a dim indoor environment under relatively soft ambient illumination. A clean image is first captured without an active reflection source. Controlled reflection sources, including a candle, flashlight, desk lamp, smartphone screen, and LED light stick, are then introduced while keeping the camera and subject approximately fixed. The reflection source is repositioned around the subject to produce spatially diverse lens reflections. Subject pose is also varied using near-frontal views, left/right head turns, and upward/downward head rotations. These controlled combinations yield 100 candidate reflected–clean pairs. For the online subset, data are collected through remote WeChat video sessions. Participants prepare common controllable light sources, such as a computer screen and desk lamp, and switch or reposition them to produce visible eyeglass reflections. Clean and reflected frames are captured from the video stream under approximately unchanged subject pose and camera viewpoint, yielding another 100 candidate reflected–clean pairs. Following the paired-data processing strategy of ReyeR [ 1 ] , we screen the candidate pairs using geometric and appearance-based consistency checks followed by manual inspection. Samples with noticeable head motion, eye or gaze changes, eyeglass-frame displacement, background shift, camera shake, or other local structural inconsistencies are removed. We then apply color-consistency correction using white-balance adjustment, histogram matching, and color transfer. After filtering and correction, 62 offline pairs and 95 online pairs are retained, resulting in 157 reference pairs. The retained clean images are used as visual references for qualitative analysis rather than as pixel-level ground truth. Their corresponding 157 reflected images are included in Ocu-R together with 301 independently collected unpaired reflected images, forming the full 458-image real-world evaluation set. From these 458 reflected inputs, 30 images are randomly sampled for the blind user study. The clean reference images are not shown to participants and are not used in the user-study evaluation.

sections.heading: A.3.2 In-the-wild Test Images
sections.text: We additionally collect 301 unpaired reflected images in unconstrained real-world environments. The images are self-captured across diverse everyday scenes, including shopping malls, subway stations, streets and intersections, supermarkets, and other outdoor locations. We use opportunistic capture: subjects wear their own eyeglasses, and each image is acquired after visually confirming the presence of lens reflection at capture time. Reflections arise naturally from surrounding illumination, including nearby artificial light sources and outdoor natural light such as low-angle sunlight around sunset. No corresponding clean image is captured for this subset. The resulting 301 images form the unpaired real-world subset of Ocu-R. The subset follows the naturally occurring variation induced by opportunistic capture, including differences in illumination, viewpoint, head pose, eyeglass appearance, reflection source, and reflection severity. These images contribute to the real-world evaluation on Ocu-R, including no-reference assessment and blind user evaluation. Representative self-collected face images are omitted from the dataset overview figure.

To standardize the spatial scale used for photometric and high-frequency measurements, images whose longer side exceeds 512 pixels are resized with preserved aspect ratio such that the longer side is 512 pixels. sections.heading: B.1 Ocular-Prior-Guided Adaptive Representation
sections.text: We provide additional details of the ocular-prior-guided representation introduced in § 4.1 . As illustrated in Fig. 10 , the reflected input is first converted into a geometry-aware importance field, from which an exact-budget quadtree determines the spatial support of each token. The resulting leaves retain both native image content and continuous geometric information for subsequent restoration. Figure 10 : Construction of the ocular-prior-guided adaptive representation. Face and iris landmarks extracted from the reflected input are used to construct geometry-derived ocular supports, which define the spatial importance field and structural constraints. An exact-budget heap solver allocates N = 256 N=256 quadtree leaves across four spatial scales, concentrating fine supports on ocular and lens regions while retaining coarse context elsewhere. The resulting leaf supports are mapped back to the native-resolution image for canonical patch sampling, while leaf geometry and pooled semantic priors provide conditioning for subsequent restoration.

For example, the lens region retains its soft refinement weight even after its hard 8 × 8 8\times 8 maximum-leaf-size constraint is relaxed. Geometry fallback. We use all available ocular cues without requiring complete iris detection. For each detected face, missing iris landmarks remove only the corresponding iris prior, while available eye and periocular supports are retained. Let A = 256 2 A=256^{2} be the logical-canvas area. Integral images for the importance field and structural supports require O ⁡ ( A ) O(A) time and memory. sections.heading: C.1.2 Inference Details
sections.text: For all reported results, we use the final EMA checkpoint. Given an input image of size H × W H\times W , OcuFlow edge-pads the shorter spatial dimension to a square canvas of side S = max ⁡ ( H , W ) S=\max(H,W) . The estimated ocular geometry is mapped to the 256 × 256 256\times 256 logical domain, where the adaptive quadtree produces N = 256 N=256 leaves. Each leaf is mapped to its corresponding support on the S × S S\times S image canvas, and its RGB content is bicubically resampled into a 24 × 24 24\times 24 canonical patch. The observation-anchored source perturbation described in § 4.2 is applied using a fixed evaluation seed. Restoration uses the endpoint setting ( r , t ) = ( 0 , 1 ) (r,t)=(0,1) and requires one restoration-network evaluation (1-NFE). The restored canonical patches are projected onto their corresponding full-resolution supports and combined with the padded observation by the frequency-preserving renderer. The padded region is then removed to recover the supplied H × W H\times W image extent. Inference uses BF16 precision.

sections.heading: C.1.3 Evaluation Protocols
sections.text: Common paired-evaluation protocol. For the paired benchmark, all methods receive inputs standardized to 1008 × 1296 1008\times 1296 using the same aspect-ratio-preserving resize-and-pad transform. Each method then applies its own internal preprocessing as required. Predictions are mapped back through the inverse external transform to the original paired-image resolution, where all full-reference metrics are computed. Evaluation rationale. Eyeglass reflections typically affect a relatively small portion of the image while directly degrading the appearance and local structure of the ocular region [ 2 ] . Consequently, full-image PSNR can be dominated by the much larger unaffected facial and background regions: because PSNR is derived from spatially averaged mean-squared error, errors within a small but task-critical eye region may contribute only weakly to the final score. This limitation is consistent with the well-established shortcomings of MSE-based fidelity measures for perceptually important image distortions [ 38 ] . We therefore report Mask-PSNR and Mask-SSIM within the eyeglass region, together with Mixed-PSNR and Mixed-SSIM to measure restoration inside the affected region while accounting for preservation elsewhere. Regional pixelwise agreement alone does not fully characterize the quality of ocular restoration. PSNR and SSIM can remain insensitive to perceptually meaningful changes in local appearance and structure [ 39 ] . We therefore additionally report Eye-ROI LPIPS for perceptual similarity and landmark-based errors for ocular geometry. This task-oriented evaluation is also motivated by prior eyeglass-reflection-removal studies, which have shown that reflections affect iris localization and facial landmark detection and have evaluated restoration through downstream iris or landmark accuracy [ 3 , 1 ] . Eye-NME and Iris-NME directly quantify displacement of eye-contour and iris landmarks relative to the clean reference, complementing the regional reconstruction and perceptual metrics. Regional PSNR and SSIM quantify reconstruction agreement within the task-relevant area, while Eye-ROI LPIPS and landmark-based errors characterize perceptual and geometric changes to the ocular structures themselves. Eye-ROI LPIPS is evaluated over a binocular region defined from clean-reference MediaPipe landmarks [ 27 ] . For each paired sample, iris landmarks detected from the clean image are converted into left- and right-iris circles and used as reference targets. The same iris-localization pipeline is independently applied to the reflected input and to the output of each restoration method. For each eye, localization accuracy is measured by the intersection-over-union (IoU) between the predicted and reference iris circles. An eye is considered correctly localized when its circle IoU is at least τ \tau . At the image level, a sample is counted as successful when both eyes satisfy the threshold. We report the bilateral localization success rate across IoU thresholds and the minimum IoU of the two eyes. All methods are evaluated using the same downstream detector without downstream fine-tuning or method-specific adaptation. Real-world metrics and blind user study. We evaluate all 458 458 Ocu-R images at their native resolutions using NIQE [ 28 ] and CLIP-IQA+ [ 29 ] . Both metrics are computed using the default PyIQA configurations from the final restored images, without additional manual resizing or normalization. We additionally conduct a blind multi-way preference study on 30 30 images randomly sampled from Ocu-R using a fixed random seed of 2026 2026 . All 133 133 participants evaluate the same 30 30 images, yielding 133 × 30 = 3,990 133\times 30=3{,}990 selections. For each trial, the original reflected input is displayed above the outputs of all nine compared methods. Method identities are hidden, and the presentation order of the nine outputs is independently randomized for each participant and image. Participants select exactly one result, with no tie option, based jointly on reflection-removal effectiveness and preservation of the original image content. All 30 30 trials are required for submission, and all 133 133 submitted questionnaires are complete. Informed consent is obtained before participation. We report each method’s overall preference share over all 3,990 3{,}990 selections and its image wins, defined as the number of test images on which it receives the largest number of participant selections. No image-level ties occur. Uncertainty in the overall preference share is estimated using a two-way bootstrap over participants and images. For each of 5,000 5{,}000 bootstrap replicates, 133 133 participants and 30 30 images are independently resampled with replacement, and the preference share is recomputed over the resulting crossed responses. The 2.5 2.5 th and 97.5 97.5 th percentiles define the reported 95 % 95\% confidence interval.

sections.heading: C.1.5 Efficiency Protocol
sections.text: All methods are benchmarked on the same NVIDIA RTX 4090 using the standardized paired-benchmark inputs defined in § C.1.3 . The common benchmark preprocessing is completed before timing. Timing covers the complete method-specific inference pipeline, including internal resizing, padding, tiling, sampling, preprocessing, and postprocessing. Three warm-up runs are excluded. Runtime is reported as the average wall-clock time per image under sustained inference. Each method uses its normal CPU–GPU parallelism and asynchronous execution during benchmarking. File encoding and disk I/O are excluded. OcuFlow is evaluated with batch size 1 1 , BF16 precision, and 1-NFE. Its timed pipeline includes ocular-geometry extraction, adaptive-grid construction, native-resolution patch sampling, canonical resampling, one-step pMF restoration, partition-of-unity projection, frequency-preserving synthesis, and final cropping. Ocular-geometry extraction uses four asynchronous CPU workers and runs concurrently with GPU inference.

sections.text: Complementary restoration and ocular gains. The results in Tab. 2 show that OcuFlow improves restoration quality, ocular perceptual fidelity, and geometric consistency simultaneously rather than optimizing a single reconstruction criterion. Among the seven paired-reference metrics, OcuFlow ranks first on six and second only on Mixed-SSIM, where it differs from the best result by 0.0004 0.0004 ( 0.7074 0.7074 versus 0.7078 0.7078 ). Compared with DSIT, the strongest competing baseline across the four reconstruction metrics, OcuFlow improves Mask-PSNR by 0.5654 0.5654 dB, Mixed-PSNR by 0.1889 0.1889 dB, and Mask-SSIM by 0.0155 0.0155 , while reducing Eye-ROI LPIPS by 29.2 % 29.2\% , Eye-NME by 8.7 % 8.7\% , and Iris-NME by 6.7 % 6.7\% . sections.heading: C.3 Downstream Iris Localization
sections.text: Figure 12 : Downstream iris-localization evaluation. (a) Both-eyes localization success rate under different iris-circle IoU thresholds. (b) Distribution of the minimum left/right iris-circle IoU for each method. Glare denotes the original reflected input without reflection removal, while OcuFlow is highlighted in red. Beyond restoration fidelity, we further examine whether eyeglass-reflection removal improves the reliability of a downstream ocular-analysis task. Specifically, we evaluate iris localization using a fixed iris-landmark detector, without method-specific adaptation or downstream fine-tuning. The goal is to assess whether the restored ocular structures are not only visually plausible, but also sufficiently consistent for subsequent vision processing. For each paired sample, iris circles estimated from the clean image are used as pseudo-ground truth. The same detector is independently applied to the reflected input and to the output of each restoration method. Let IoU left \operatorname{IoU}_{\mathrm{left}} and IoU right \operatorname{IoU}_{\mathrm{right}} denote the circle IoUs of the two eyes. We define the image-level localization score as s iris = min ⁡ ( IoU left , IoU right ) s_{\mathrm{iris}}=\min\left(\operatorname{IoU}_{\mathrm{left}},\operatorname{IoU}_{\mathrm{right}}\right) , such that an image is considered successfully localized at threshold τ \tau only when s iris ≥ τ s_{\mathrm{iris}}\geq\tau . This conservative criterion requires both eyes to be accurately localized. As shown in Fig. 12 (a), eyeglass reflections substantially degrade downstream iris localization, with the original reflected input exhibiting a markedly lower success rate over a broad range of IoU thresholds. Reflection removal recovers a large portion of this lost localization performance, while OcuFlow remains among the strongest methods throughout the moderate-to-high threshold range. At the default threshold τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 , OcuFlow achieves a both-eyes localization success rate of 85.30 % 85.30\% , compared with 54.43 % 54.43\% for the reflected input and 83.78 % 83.78\% for the strongest competing method, DSIT. This corresponds to a 30.87 30.87 percentage-point improvement over the unprocessed reflected input. Fig. 12 (b) further examines the distribution of the minimum left/right iris IoU, which reflects the localization quality of the more difficult eye in each image. OcuFlow exhibits a clear rightward shift relative to the reflected input and achieves a median minimum IoU of 0.765 0.765 . This distributional improvement indicates that the downstream gain is not restricted to a single operating threshold, but instead reflects more consistently recovered iris geometry across the evaluation set. These results complement Eye-NME and Iris-NME by measuring functional downstream utility rather than geometric error alone. While the landmark-based metrics quantify agreement with the clean reference, the downstream localization experiment directly evaluates whether a fixed ocular-analysis pipeline can reliably operate on the restored images. The results therefore show that reflection removal restores task-relevant iris structure, with OcuFlow providing strong overall downstream localization performance.

sections.heading: C.4.1 Qualitative comparison.
sections.text: Across Figs. 13 – 15 , the competing methods exhibit several recurring types of restoration error. ER 2 Net [ 1 ] and DSRNet [ 31 ] often suppress the strongest reflection response while leaving residual glare or reduced contrast within the lens region. Under stronger occlusion, the recovered iris and eyelid boundaries can remain less distinct than in the clean reference. DSIT [ 33 ] and ReflexSplit [ 35 ] generally remove a larger fraction of the visible reflection, but several examples exhibit smoother ocular appearance and attenuated local contrast. RDNet [ 34 ] frequently retains sharper local structure, although blue or purple chromatic residuals remain around the iris or lens region in multiple cases. Stable Diffusion 1.5 [ 30 ] and Stable Diffusion 3.5 [ 32 ] can substantially alter local color, contrast, or facial appearance beyond the original reflection pattern. DL2G [ 2 ] preserves global facial appearance well in several examples but can introduce locally inconsistent structures around the eyeglass rims and eyelid boundaries. These differences become particularly visible for saturated highlights, broad colored reflections, and glare overlapping the pupil or iris. In such cases, incomplete suppression leaves visible contamination, while stronger correction can introduce smoothing, chromatic shifts, or local structural changes. Across the shown examples, OcuFlow more closely follows the clean references in both the spatial extent of the correction and the recovered ocular appearance. Localized glare is removed while eyeglass boundaries and surrounding facial texture remain stable, and strongly colored reflections are restored with fewer persistent chromatic residuals. Under severe ocular occlusion, the recovered iris position, eyelid contour, and local eye contrast remain closer to the clean reference than the smoother or more strongly altered outputs observed in several competing methods. These comparisons illustrate the restoration–preservation trade-off in eyeglass reflection removal: effective suppression of corrupted content should be accompanied by preservation of ocular geometry and reliable local detail. Figure 16 : Ocular-prior-guided selective restoration. In the upper example, the eyeglasses are displaced away from the visible eyes, and OcuFlow leaves the lens appearance largely unchanged. In the lower example, a strong reflection overlaps the eye; OcuFlow applies stronger correction to the ocularly relevant region while making smaller changes to surrounding lens reflections.

sections.heading: C.4.2 Ocular-prior-guided selective restoration.
sections.text: Fig. 16 illustrates the spatial selectivity induced by the ocular prior. In the upper example, the eyeglasses are displaced above the eyes, so the visible lens reflections do not overlap the ocular structures. OcuFlow consequently leaves the input largely unchanged. Several competing methods modify the lens regions more extensively, producing partial reflection suppression, local contrast changes, or irregular residual structures. In this example, DSIT and ReflexSplit introduce eye-like ghosting patterns within the lenses, while DL2G produces noticeable local texture distortion. The lower example presents the complementary case. A strong bright reflection overlaps the left eye and obscures useful ocular detail, whereas the larger reflections near the upper parts of the lenses lie mostly outside the visible eye regions. OcuFlow applies stronger restoration around the affected eye while making smaller changes to the surrounding lens appearance. Several competing methods show broader or less localized changes: ER 2 Net and DSRNet retain visible degradation around the ocular region, SD3.5 substantially alters the overall lens appearance, and DL2G leaves a strong bright residual near the eye together with local structural artifacts. These examples illustrate how the ocular prior modulates the spatial extent of restoration according to the relationship between lens reflections and visible ocular structures. The resulting behavior reduces unnecessary changes to lens regions that do not interfere with eye visibility while concentrating stronger correction on reflections that overlap the eyes.

sections.heading: C.4.3 Failure cases.
sections.text: Figure 17 : Failure case on sunglasses. OcuFlow reconstructs visible eye content behind the intentionally dark lenses, deviating from the clean reference. OcuFlow can fail on sunglasses, where reduced ocular visibility is caused by intrinsic lens attenuation rather than reflection alone. As shown in Fig. 17 , the ocular-restoration prior encourages reconstruction of visible eye content behind the dark lenses, leading to a result that deviates from the clean reference. This failure mode indicates that future models should better distinguish reflection-induced occlusion from intrinsic lens properties such as dark tint or strong attenuation.

Dashed lines separate input (Reflection) and restored (Removal) regions, with complementary comparisons across both rows. 1 Introduction Reflections from windows or monitors on eyeglasses can obscure the eyes while leaving most of a portrait intact. Although spatially confined, this interference can noticeably change facial appearance in photographs and video communication. Its effects range from color shifts over visible structures to severe occlusion of the iris, eyelids, and eyelashes [ 1 , 2 ] . A single image may therefore require photometric correction in some regions, content reconstruction in others, and faithful preservation elsewhere. Accommodating these different restoration needs is essential to removing reflections without unnecessarily changing the portrait. Despite progress in eyeglass reflection removal [ 3 , 1 , 2 ] , challenges remain in obtaining reliable supervision and evaluation data and balancing restoration accuracy with inference efficiency. At the data level, limitations are threefold: (1) head motion, blinking, and illumination changes compromise pixel-level correspondence in captured pairs [ 1 ] ; (2) synthetic pairs provide controlled correspondence and degradation but cannot alone establish performance under natural reflections; and (3) real-input pseudo-pairs retain natural reflections, but the true appearance of obscured ocular content cannot be verified from reflected inputs alone. Therefore, reliable assessment requires complementary sources and real-world evaluation independent of generated targets. At the model level, reconstructing obscured ocular structures requires expressive priors, while applications demand efficient inference. Diffusion models [ 4 ] , DiT [ 5 ] , and SiT [ 6 ] demonstrate strong image synthesis capabilities. These models typically rely on iterative sampling with multiple network evaluations. MeanFlow [ 7 ] learns average velocities over time intervals for single-evaluation generation, while pMF [ 8 ] combines image prediction with velocity-space learning for one-step generation without a latent autoencoder. Although pMF provides an efficient foundation for one-step generation, applying it to eyeglass reflection removal requires aligning generative computation with spatially heterogeneous restoration demands. Under a limited token budget, uniform tokenization allocates computation to largely unaffected regions while providing insufficient resolution for fine ocular structures. Within the lenses, similar reflection intensities may leave different amounts of ocular structure visible, indicating that reflection strength alone cannot determine restoration requirements. Therefore, effective reconstruction requires guidance from both local observations and ocular geometry. In addition, compact patch representations can discard native photographic details, whereas directly preserving observed high-frequency content risks retaining reflection artifacts. To address these challenges, we introduce OcuBench , a multi-source benchmark for eyeglass reflection removal. OcuBench comprises 10,280 synthetic pairs, 732 real-input pseudo-pairs, and 458 independently collected real-world test images. Synthetic pairs vary in subject, imaging, and reflection factors. Real-input pseudo-pairs combine real reflected inputs with generated clean targets. The real-world set evaluates performance beyond generated supervision, with clean references for a subset. These sources support development and evaluation under controlled and real-world conditions. Based on OcuBench, we develop OcuFlow , an efficient ocular-adaptive pMF framework for eyeglass reflection removal. OcuFlow uses geometry-adaptive supports under a fixed token budget to concentrate resolution on ocular structures while preserving coarse context. The supports retain position and scale information to preserve spatial correspondence. A geometry-guided pMF integrates local reflected observations, ocular priors, and cross-scale features to restore pixel patches in one forward pass. A native-resolution frequency-preserving renderer projects predictions to the supplied input resolution. The renderer selectively blends predictions with observations across frequency bands to preserve photographic details and reduce unnecessary modifications. Experiments show that OcuFlow achieves superior overall restoration quality on the held-out paired benchmark compared with existing methods. OcuFlow runs in 56 ms per image on an RTX 4090 GPU, providing 4 4 – 66 × 66\times speedups over the compared methods under the same evaluation protocol. Independent real-world evaluation further shows competitive no-reference performance, and OcuFlow achieves the highest user preference in the user study. Beyond image-level restoration metrics, we evaluate downstream iris localization using a fixed detector without fine-tuning. OcuFlow achieves the best both-eyes localization accuracy among the compared method, demonstrating that its restoration benefits extend to downstream ocular analysis. These results demonstrate the potential of OcuFlow for efficient and detail-preserving portrait restoration. 2 Related Work Eyeglass Reflection Removal and Benchmarks. EwE [ 3 ] overlays reflection patches on frontal portraits, while De-Glared [ 9 ] constructs 2,541 synthetic pairs from generated portraits. ReyeR [ 1 ] provides filtered, color-corrected real pairs across varied conditions. Synthetic realism and real-pair alignment remain challenges. Methods span constrained optimization [ 3 ] , supervised restoration [ 10 , 9 ] , and generative facial reconstruction [ 11 ] . ER 2 Net [ 1 ] fuses reflection removal and inpainting by reflection intensity, while DL2G [ 2 ] combines degradation correction, local structure-aware diffusion, and global refinement. We introduce a multi-source benchmark and efficient restoration for portrait editing and video communication. Spatially Adaptive Visual Representations. Adaptive visual representations improve efficiency through token aggregation, conditional computation, and spatially varying resolution. TokenLearner [ 12 ] aggregates dense features into fewer adaptive tokens, while A-ViT [ 13 ] dynamically halts token processing at different network depths. Mixed-Resolution Tokenization [ 14 ] constructs variable-sized patches through saliency-guided quadtree partitioning, whereas MSViT [ 15 ] uses learned gating to select patch scales with input-dependent token counts. For eyeglass restoration, spatial allocation must resolve fine ocular structures while maintaining correspondence with the original image. OcuFlow uses input-derived ocular geometry to optimize quadtree partitioning under a fixed token budget, concentrating resolution on critical eye structures. Each token retains its position and scale for geometry-guided restoration and native-resolution reconstruction. Generative Restoration. Generative priors support restoration from incomplete observations. Diffusion [ 4 ] and Flow Matching [ 16 ] typically require iterative sampling. DifFace [ 17 ] reconstructs faces with pretrained diffusion, while DiffBIR [ 18 ] combines degradation removal with diffusion-based detail regeneration. GFP-GAN [ 19 ] enables single-pass restoration using pretrained facial GAN priors. CodeFormer [ 20 ] predicts discrete codes with a controllable fidelity–quality trade-off. Dereflection Any Image [ 21 ] adopts one-step diffusion for reflection removal. MeanFlow [ 7 ] learns average velocities over time intervals for single-evaluation generation. pMF [ 8 ] combines image prediction with velocity-space learning for one-step pixel-space generation. We adapt it to conditional restoration over ocular-adaptive patches. One-step restoration addresses efficiency , but not what to restore and preserve . WaveFace [ 22 ] uses diffusion for low-frequency wavelet components and a feed-forward network for high-frequency recovery. Our renderer blends predictions with native-resolution observations by frequency, selectively retaining reliable high-frequency details beyond compact patches. We acquire 200 candidate reflected–clean pairs through controlled offline photography and online video conferencing, with the reflection-inducing light enabled and disabled. We collect 301 unpaired images from unconstrained environments, covering varied illumination, viewpoints, eyeglasses, and reflection conditions. For the SoF dataset, CLIP-based reflection screening [ 25 ] followed by manual inspection yields 199 images. The resulting 732 images are used to generate pseudo-clean targets. Ocu-S and Ocu-P Validation. GPT-Image-2 generates synthetic pairs under shared scene constraints, whereas real-input editing must preserve the photograph while inferring obscured content. Of the 200 candidate pairs, 157 are retained, comprising 62 offline and 95 video-conferencing pairs. Residual local misalignment remains, so the clean captures serve as visual references rather than pixel-accurate ground truth. Together with the 301 unpaired images, these form the 458-image Ocu-R. OcuBench combines synthetic pairs, real-input pseudo-pairs, and independent real-world evaluation beyond generated targets. OcuFlow aligns a fixed token budget with ocular geometry and couples one-step restoration with frequency-preserving synthesis to reconstruct obscured eyes while retaining reliable native details. Experiments demonstrate improved reflection removal and ocular-structure reconstruction, leading to more accurate downstream iris localization, while achieving favorable human perceptual preferences on independent real-world images at substantially lower inference cost. Our findings suggest that adapting representation to local needs and selectively preserving observations support effective one-step portrait restoration.
